stimulus.text: Paraphrase: In November 1942, American troops under General Dwight D. Eisenhower landed in Morocco and Algeria, the first American offensive against Nazi-held territory. Moving east, they joined British forces driving west, and by May 1943 all of North Africa was in Allied hands. The Allies then landed in Sicily in July 1943 and in Italy that September. Churchill had called Italy the 'soft underbelly' of the Axis, but German troops fought for every mile, and Rome did not fall until June 1944.
stimulus.source_note: Original secondary summary drawn from Barron's Chapter 9 ('Fighting in North Africa'; 'The Soft Underbelly of the Axis') and 5 Steps Chapter 24.

source: original; stimulus drawn from book-grounded figures and paraphrases (see source_note)
stem: Why did Roosevelt and Churchill choose North Africa and Italy before attempting an invasion of France?

options.text: They wanted to fight Germany somewhere without invading France before the Allies were ready
Stalin demanded that the Allies invade North Africa instead of France
options.misconception: Stalin wanted a second front in France; North Africa was the Allies' choice, not his.

options.text: German troops had already withdrawn from France by the year 1942
options.misconception: German troops held France until the Normandy landings in 1944.

options.text: The United States had no troops available for an invasion of France in 1942
options.misconception: American troops were available; they landed in North Africa in November 1942.

rationales.A: The Allies opened a front in North Africa while building up for France.
rationales.B: Stalin pressed for a landing in France, not for North Africa.
rationales.C: German troops held France until D-Day in June 1944.
rationales.D: American troops were available; they landed in North Africa in November 1942.
rationales.general:
1. Background from the books: Churchill opposed invading France at once, fearing a repeat of the trench warfare of World War I.
2. Roosevelt and Churchill agreed instead to open a front in North Africa, then Italy.
3. Those campaigns gave the Allies experience and tied down German troops.
4. The invasion of France waited until June 1944, when the Allies were ready.
Remember: when an invasion is delayed, look for the safer front the Allies chose instead.
